title: Canadian RRSP vs US 401(k): Complete Tax Comparison for Cross-Border Workers
description: Comprehensive comparison of RRSP vs 401(k) for H-1B and TN visa holders. Covers contribution limits, tax treatment, withdrawal rules, cross-border implications, and optimization strategies.
content:
## Key Takeaways

- RRSP and 401(k) are tax-deferred retirement accounts (contribute pre-tax, pay tax on withdrawal)
- 401(k) has higher contribution limits: $23,500 vs RRSP's 18% of income (max ~$31,560 CAD)
- 401(k) has employer match (50-100% of first 6%) — free money you must take
- RRSP is treaty-protected in the US (no tax on earnings until withdrawal)
- 401(k) is NOT treaty-protected in Canada (requires annual T1135 reporting + complex tax treatment)
- Cross-border workers should prioritize 401(k) while in US, RRSP when back in Canada

## What Are RRSP and 401(k)?

### Canadian RRSP (Registered Retirement Savings Plan)

**How it works:**
- You contribute pre-tax dollars (reduces taxable income)
- Contribution limit: 18% of prior year income, max $31,560 CAD (2026)
- Unused room carries forward indefinitely
- Investments grow tax-free
- Pay tax when you withdraw (presumably in retirement at lower tax rate)

**Example:**
- 2025 income: $100,000 CAD
- 2026 RRSP limit: $18,000 CAD
- You contribute $18,000 → saves $6,300 tax (35% marginal rate)
- Grow to $100,000 by retirement
- Withdraw $20,000/year → pay 20% tax ($4,000)
- **Net savings: $6,300 - $4,000 = $2,300** (plus 30 years of tax-free growth)

### US 401(k)

**How it works:**
- You contribute pre-tax dollars via payroll deduction
- Contribution limit: $23,500 (2026), plus $7,500 catch-up if age 50+
- Employer match: Typically 50-100% of first 3-6% of salary
- Investments grow tax-free
- Pay tax when you withdraw (age 59.5+, or penalties apply)

**Example:**
- Salary: $150,000
- You contribute: 10% = $15,000
- Employer match: 50% of first 6% = $4,500 (free money!)
- Total contribution: $19,500
- Tax savings: $15,000 × 32% = $4,800
- **Instant return: $4,500 match + $4,800 tax savings = $9,300 on $15,000 invested (62% return!)**

### Roth Variants: TFSA vs Roth 401(k)

**TFSA (Tax-Free Savings Account):**
- Contribute AFTER-tax dollars
- Withdrawals are tax-free
- Contribution limit: $7,000/year (2026)
- **Problem for US residents:** IRS treats TFSA as a "foreign trust" (not tax-free in US)

**Roth 401(k):**
- Contribute AFTER-tax dollars
- Withdrawals are tax-free (after age 59.5)
- Same contribution limit as traditional 401(k) ($23,500)
- **Problem for Canadian residents:** Canada doesn't recognize Roth (taxes withdrawals as income)

## Side-by-Side Comparison

| Feature | RRSP | 401(k) |
|---------|------|--------|
| **Contribution limit (2026)** | 18% of income, max $31,560 CAD | $23,500 USD (~$32,000 CAD) |
| **Employer match** | No (except group RRSPs) | Yes (typical: 3-6% of salary) |
| **Tax deduction** | Contribution deductible in Canada | Contribution deductible in US |
| **Taxation on growth** | Tax-free until withdrawal | Tax-free until withdrawal |
| **Early withdrawal penalty** | No penalty, but full tax owed | 10% penalty + tax (before age 59.5) |
| **Mandatory withdrawals** | RRIF at age 71 | RMD at age 73 |
| **Portability** | Stays in Canada (even if you move) | Stays in US (even if you move) |
| **Cross-border tax treaty** | Protected in US (Article XVIII) | NOT protected in Canada |
| **Borrowing (home purchase)** | $35,000 via Home Buyers' Plan | No borrowing allowed |
| **Investment options** | Any investment (stocks, bonds, GICs) | Limited to employer's plan options |

## Cross-Border Tax Treatment

### RRSP While Living in the US (H-1B/TN Worker)

**The Good News: Treaty Protection**

Article XVIII of the Canada-US tax treaty allows you to defer US tax on RRSP earnings.

**How to claim:**
- File **Form 8891** (or attach statement to Form 1040)
- Elect to defer taxation under treaty
- Report RRSP contributions, earnings, withdrawals
- Earnings are NOT taxed annually (unlike foreign mutual funds)

**Example:**
- RRSP balance: $100,000 CAD
- 2026 investment income: $7,000
- **US tax: $0** (treaty protection)
- **Canadian tax: $0** (RRSP is tax-deferred)

Without treaty election:
- US would tax $7,000 as ordinary income → $2,240 tax (32% bracket)

**Reporting requirements:**
- **Form 8938 (FATCA):** Report if RRSP > $50k (single) or $100k (married)
- **FBAR (FinCEN 114):** Report if total foreign accounts > $10k

**Can you contribute to RRSP while in the US?**

**Yes, but:**
- Contribution is tax-deductible in Canada (saves ~35% Canadian tax)
- NOT deductible in US (but earnings are treaty-protected)
- Makes sense if you plan to return to Canada (withdraw at lower rate)

### 401(k) While Living in Canada (Returned to Canada)

**The Bad News: No Treaty Protection**

Canada does NOT recognize 401(k) under the tax treaty. It's treated as a regular foreign investment account.

**Tax treatment:**
- Annual earnings are taxable in Canada (interest, dividends, capital gains)
- Must report on **Form T1135** (Foreign Income Verification Statement)
- Withdrawals are taxed as foreign pension income (eligible for pension credit)

**Example:**
- 401(k) balance: $500,000 USD
- 2026 investment income: $35,000 (7% return)
- **Canadian tax: $12,250** (35% marginal rate)
- **US tax: $0** (no US tax until withdrawal)

**Withdrawal complications:**
- US withholds 30% (non-resident rate)
- Canada taxes full amount as income (15% federal pension credit)
- You claim Foreign Tax Credit for US withholding

**Example:**
- Withdraw $50,000 USD from 401(k)
- US withholding: 30% = $15,000
- You receive: $35,000
- Canadian tax: $50,000 × 35% = $17,500
- Foreign Tax Credit: -$15,000
- **Net Canadian tax: $2,500**
- **Total tax: $17,500** (35% effective rate)

**Roth 401(k) in Canada:**

**Even worse:**
- Canada doesn't recognize Roth (no treaty provision)
- Withdrawals are taxed as foreign income (NOT tax-free)
- You paid tax on contributions in US, now pay tax again in Canada

**Example:**
- Roth 401(k): $300,000 (all after-tax contributions)
- Withdraw $50,000
- US tax: $0 (Roth is tax-free in US)
- **Canadian tax: $17,500** (35% rate, no tax credit because US didn't withhold)

**Double taxation!**

### Optimal Strategy for Cross-Border Workers

**Phase 1: Working in US (H-1B/TN)**

✅ **Prioritize 401(k):**
- Max out to employer match (free money)
- Contribute up to $23,500/year
- Tax deduction reduces US tax by $7,520 (32% bracket)

✅ **Keep existing RRSP but don't contribute:**
- File Form 8891 to defer US tax on earnings
- Let it grow tax-free
- Report on Form 8938 and FBAR

❌ **Don't contribute to RRSP (while in US):**
- No US tax deduction (only Canadian)
- Better to max 401(k) first

**Phase 2: Returning to Canada**

✅ **Stop contributing to 401(k):**
- You can't contribute once you leave the employer
- Let it sit and grow (but pay Canadian tax on earnings)

✅ **Max out RRSP:**
- You're back in Canada → full tax deduction
- Contribution room carries forward from all prior years
- Example: 10 years of unused room = $180,000 contribution potential

✅ **Consider 401(k) to RRSP rollover:**
- Some cross-border CPAs can structure this (complex)
- Avoids annual Canadian tax on 401(k) earnings
- But triggers US tax on full 401(k) balance (not ideal)

**Phase 3: Retirement (Living in Canada)**

✅ **Withdraw 401(k) strategically:**
- Withdraw in low-income years (25% bracket)
- Claim Foreign Tax Credit for US withholding
- Coordinate with RRSP withdrawals (RRIF mandatory at 71)

✅ **Convert 401(k) to RRIF (if possible):**
- CRA may recognize 401(k) as foreign pension
- Allows income splitting with spouse
- Qualifies for pension income credit ($2,000 federal)

## Real-World Scenarios

### Scenario 1: TN Visa Worker (3 Years in US)

**Profile:**
- Sarah, 28, software engineer from Vancouver
- TN visa, working in Seattle 2024-2027
- Salary: $140,000 USD
- Canadian RRSP: $60,000 (from before US move)
- Plans to return to Canada in 2027

**Strategy:**

**401(k) contributions (while in US):**
- Contribute 15% of salary: $21,000/year
- Employer match (50% of 6%): $4,200/year
- Total: $25,200/year × 3 years = **$75,600**
- Tax savings: $21,000 × 24% × 3 = $15,120

**RRSP (keep but don't contribute):**
- Balance grows from $60k → $78k (7%/year × 3 years)
- US tax on earnings: $0 (treaty protected via Form 8891)
- Report on FBAR and Form 8938

**After returning to Canada (2027):**
- 401(k) balance: $75,600 + growth = ~$90,000
- Canadian tax on 401(k) earnings: ~$2,200/year (7% × 35% tax)
- RRSP: Contribute $25,000/year (max out Canadian deduction)

**Retirement (age 65):**
- 401(k) grew to $800,000 USD
- RRSP grew to $1,200,000 CAD
- Withdraw both strategically (25% tax bracket)
- Use Foreign Tax Credit to offset 401(k) US withholding

**Total tax paid over lifetime:**
- US: $15,120 saved (401k deductions)
- Canada: $78,000 paid (withdrawals at 25%)
- **Effective tax rate: 20%** (vs 35% without planning)

### Scenario 2: H-1B Worker (Permanent US Move)

**Profile:**
- David, 35, from Toronto
- H-1B → Green Card (2025)
- Salary: $200,000
- Canadian RRSP: $150,000 (from before US move)

**Strategy:**

**Mistake to avoid:**
- Don't keep contributing to RRSP (no US tax benefit)
- Don't convert RRSP to 401(k) (loses treaty protection)

**Optimal approach:**

1. **Max 401(k) in US:**
   - $23,500/year + $10,000 employer match = $33,500
   - Tax savings: $23,500 × 35% = $8,225/year

2. **Keep RRSP, file Form 8891:**
   - Let it grow tax-deferred
   - Withdraw after age 71 (mandatory RRIF withdrawals)
   - Coordinate with 401(k) withdrawals (stay in 22% bracket)

3. **At retirement (living in US):**
   - Withdraw RRSP/RRIF (15% Canadian withholding)
   - Claim Foreign Tax Credit on US 1040
   - Net US tax: ~10% (after FTC)
   - Total tax: 25% (15% CA + 10% US net)

**Retirement income:**
- 401(k): $1.5M → Withdraw $60k/year (22% US tax = $13,200)
- RRSP: $500k CAD → Withdraw $20k/year (15% CA withholding = $3k, net US tax $1k)
- **Total income: $80k, total tax: $17.2k (21.5% rate)**

### Scenario 3: Frequent Cross-Border Moves

**Profile:**
- Alex, 42, consultant
- Works 2-3 years in US, then 2-3 years in Canada (repeating)
- Accumulated:
  - 401(k): $400,000 USD
  - RRSP: $300,000 CAD

**Challenge:**
- Annual tax on 401(k) earnings while in Canada: $9,800 (35% on $28k growth)
- Complex reporting (Form 8891, FBAR, Form 8938, T1135)

**Strategy:**

**Option 1: Consolidate to RRSP**
- Withdraw 401(k) over 3 years while in Canada (low-income years)
- Pay 25% Canadian tax (vs 35% on annual earnings)
- Contribute to RRSP (deduct at 35%)
- **Net tax: 0%** (withdrawal tax offset by RRSP deduction)

**Option 2: Keep both, optimize withdrawals**
- Retire in US (where 401(k) is more favorable)
- Withdraw RRSP first (while in low US bracket)
- Claim Foreign Tax Credit
- Later, withdraw 401(k) (no foreign withholding)

**Option 3: Roth conversions (complex)**
- Convert 401(k) to Roth 401(k) while in low-income year
- Pay US tax on conversion (22% bracket)
- Move to Canada with Roth (grows tax-free in US, but taxed in Canada)
- **Warning:** Roth is NOT treaty-protected in Canada

## Common Mistakes

### Mistake #1: Not Taking Employer 401(k) Match

**The error:** You don't contribute to 401(k) because you plan to return to Canada.

**The cost:**
- Free money left on table: $5,000/year × 5 years = $25,000
- Growth over 30 years (7%): $190,000

**The fix:**
- ALWAYS contribute enough to get full employer match
- It's an instant 50-100% return
- Even with Canadian tax on earnings, it's worth it

### Mistake #2: Contributing to TFSA While US Resident

**The error:** You think TFSA = Roth IRA (both tax-free).

**The cost:**
- IRS treats TFSA as foreign trust (Form 3520 required)
- Penalty: 35% of TFSA balance ($17,500 on $50k account)
- Plus FBAR penalty: $10,000

**The fix:**
- Close TFSA before becoming US resident
- Move funds to RRSP (treaty-protected) or Roth IRA

### Mistake #3: Not Filing Form 8891 (RRSP Treaty Election)

**The error:** You have an RRSP but don't file Form 8891.

**The cost:**
- US taxes RRSP earnings as ordinary income
- $5,000 earnings × 32% = $1,600 tax
- Multiply by 10 years = $16,000 overpaid

**The fix:**
- File Form 8891 (or attach statement to 1040)
- Elect treaty deferral (Article XVIII)
- Update annually

### Mistake #4: Early 401(k) Withdrawal (Before 59.5)

**The error:** You return to Canada, need cash, withdraw 401(k) at age 45.

**The cost:**
- US: 10% early withdrawal penalty + 25% tax = 35%
- Canada: 35% tax (no penalty, but full taxation)
- Foreign Tax Credit: Offset US tax
- **Net tax: 35% + 10% penalty = 45%**

**The fix:**
- Borrow against 401(k) (if plan allows)
- Use RRSP Home Buyers' Plan ($35k loan)
- Delay withdrawal until 59.5

## Optimization Strategies

### Strategy 1: Tax Bracket Arbitrage

**Concept:** Contribute in high-tax years, withdraw in low-tax years.

**Example:**
- Age 30-40: Earn $200k (35% bracket)
- Contribute $23,500/year to 401(k)
- Tax savings: $8,225/year

- Age 65-75: Retire with $50k/year income (12% bracket)
- Withdraw $23,500/year from 401(k)
- Tax paid: $2,820/year

**Net savings: $5,405/year × 10 years = $54,050**

### Strategy 2: Geographic Arbitrage

**Concept:** Withdraw retirement funds in low-tax jurisdiction.

**Example:**
- Retire in Canada (federal + provincial = 25% combined on $50k income)
- vs retiring in California (federal + state = 35% on $50k income)

**Savings: 10 percentage points = $5,000/year**

**Bonus:** Canada has better healthcare (free) and social benefits in retirement.

### Strategy 3: Income Splitting (Canada Only)

**Concept:** Split pension income with spouse (if they're in lower bracket).

**Example:**
- You: $80k pension income (35% bracket)
- Spouse: $0 income

**Without splitting:**
- Your tax: $28,000 (35% on $80k)
- Spouse tax: $0
- **Total: $28,000**

**With splitting:**
- You: $40k (25% bracket) = $10,000
- Spouse: $40k (25% bracket) = $10,000
- **Total: $20,000**
- **Savings: $8,000/year**

**How:**
- File Form T1032 (Joint Election to Split Pension Income)
- Eligible sources: RRIF, 401(k) if recognized as foreign pension

## Action Items

**If you're in the US now (H-1B/TN):**
- [ ] Max employer 401(k) match (free money)
- [ ] Contribute up to $23,500/year to 401(k)
- [ ] File Form 8891 for Canadian RRSP (defer US tax on earnings)
- [ ] Don't contribute to RRSP (unless planning to return to Canada soon)
- [ ] Don't open/contribute to TFSA (35% penalty risk)

**If you're back in Canada:**
- [ ] Max out RRSP contributions (18% of income)
- [ ] Use accumulated contribution room from years in US
- [ ] File Form T1135 for US 401(k) (if >$100k CAD)
- [ ] Plan 401(k) withdrawal strategy (age 59.5+, coordinate with RRSP)

**Before cross-border move:**
- [ ] Calculate tax impact of 401(k) earnings if moving to Canada
- [ ] Consider Roth conversion (if moving to US permanently)
- [ ] Review treaty position (Form 8891 for RRSP, no treaty for 401(k) in Canada)
